The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Forsyth, William” (tax_1833_032, line 84). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Forsyth' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

merge_ruling.for_merge: THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS CARRY ONE WILLIAM OF THE STEM AND SPELL HIM TWO WAYS, A YEAR APART AND NEVER ON ONE ROLL — which is the exact shape the Pearson fold rested part of its weight on. The tax list of the Town of Chicago for 1833 prints 'Forsyth, William' (voter_lists_1833_1835.txt line 84); the poll filed 11 August 1834 prints 'Forsythe, William' (line 210). Each of those rolls enters a man once, neither enters both spellings, and the spelling changes between them. The Chicago Democrat of 29 October 1834 then prints 'William Forsyth' in the town. The town holds exactly one William of each spelling and no other bearer of either stem.
merge_ruling.against_merge: THE ONE DOCUMENT THAT SETS BOTH IS A TRANSCRIPTION OF TWO ORIGINALS, WHICH IS THE THING C9 REFUSES TO COUNT. IRAD's 'Early Chicago Voters' PDF holds the 1833 tax list and the 1834 poll between one pair of covers, so a reader can point at one file and see both spellings — but the Pruyne ruling one cluster's-worth of reasoning above already drew this line, and it draws it the same way here: a republisher's inconsistency across two documents is not a printer's inconsistency inside one. Outside the rolls the corpus only ever sets the short form for this man: the Democrat prints Forsyth eleven times across the 1833-1835 run and Forsythe never, and Fergus 1839 prints Forsyth alone. AND ONE TITLE IS CAUGHT TREATING THE TWO AS TWO SURNAMES: the Second Presbyterian Church roll of 1892 populates both, 'Forsyth, Benjamin H. / Daniel S. / Logan Wallace / Robert / Mrs. Kate / Miss Minnie L.' and 'Forsythe, Mrs. Fannie E. / Geo. A. / Frank W. / Miss Jennie / John / Mrs. John' — thirteen people, not one William among them, and the volume alphabetises them as two names. That is not D5 (no closed roll enters both as separate entries for this forename) but it is the corpus declining to hand over the demonstration. D7, and the cards stay two. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT IS NOT A PAGE BUT A COUNT, in C12's shape moved from the forename to the surname — the closed roll leaves the documented man exactly one entry he can be, and the exhaustion is worked over the whole roll and printed rather than asserted. C12 as written reaches a FORENAME only, so firing it on a surname is itself a rule to write. T-1135 owns that question for Pruyne/Pryne and the rule it writes is the one this pair waits on.

It is evidence about 1839, written here as 1839's and read back onto no 1835 claim. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. The value is the volume's own line, split by its crosswalk on the entry's punctuation. These volumes set the trade first and its qualifiers after it on the same line, so the split may carry an employer, a market or a corner along with the trade. The printed entry is quoted beside the value for exactly that reason: the split is checkable against it, and neither is read into an 1835 claim.
